title: Tim James: Obscure and mostly moribund grape crosses in Cape vineyards

The post Tim James: Obscure and mostly moribund grape crosses in Cape vineyards appeared first on winemag.
content:
I was pleased to see Malu Lambert report, in her piece on palomino, that Adi Badenhorst is “propagating” colomino, a local cross of palomino and colombar. It seems to have been a largely unappreciated variety since some boffin in a lab had thought it a good idea and sent it through all the hoops to get to market. Perhaps it will still prove to have been a good idea. But I had once, looking at the changing shape of the Cape vineyard this century, wistfully hoped Adi would take up the claims of an equally obscure cross called brakboseiland, which I think would somehow have better suited his beard and sense of humour. Incidentally, there appears to be a pretty nondescript geographical feature in the Northern Cape with this name, presumably with some connection to the grape.

Unfortunately, however, brakboseiland has disappeared from the list of permitted vine cultivars, as per the latest update of the Wine of Origin Scheme. Actually, colomino is not there either, so, according to my understanding, Adi couldn’t sell any wine under that name until it’s reinstated. If I look at the list of plantings for 2010, I see that Brakboseiland had no plantings recorded, while there had been 0.75 hectares of the stuff ten years earlier. And colomino was moving in the same direction: 4.58 ha in 2010, down from 16.03. A further decline left only 0.03 ha in 2025 (I wonder if those are Adi’s vines?).

The vanishing crosses

Looking through those lists of vinifera grape varieties, one is struck by the number of the more obscure names that refer to deliberate grape crosses – that is, varieties intentionally created by the wine industry, rather than having emerged and been selected over centuries of “natural”, spontaneous life in the vineyards. The aim of such crosses is to combine different characteristics, frequently high quality and high productivity, but also resistance to temperature and disease. (NB, these are not hybrids – that term refers to crosses between different species, with an offspring that is, in this case, not part of the vinifera species.)

Some in the list refer to crosses created elsewhere – ruby cabernet, for example, which was bred in California from cabernet sauvignon (for quality) and carignan (productivity and heat tolerance), and is still the ninth-most-planted variety here. But most crosses on the list (and increasingly falling off it, it seems) are local creations. By far the best known, of course, is pinotage, which is locally and internationally unusual for being a cross that is widely regarded as a grape that can and does produce high-quality wine. And also for being so successful, comfortably in the top half-dozen plantings here and generally on the up, rather than the down.

Decline is a far more common story for even the most successful of deliberate crosses: Müller-Thurgau, bred at Geisenheim Grape Breeding Institute in Germany in the late 19th century from riesling and madeleine royale (though it took later DNA research to ascertain madeleine’s role), has been widely and intensively planted round the world to cover great areas (but never tried here as far as I know), although hectarage was markedly in decline in recent decades.

After pinotage, the highest place for a local cross on our list is nouvelle, jogging along at around 360 ha. Bred from crouchen and ugni blanc by Chris Orffer (our preeminent grape breeder, who clearly enjoyed the process), it dates back some 60 years, but took off in a small way this century. In 2000 there was less than 2 ha of it, but someone no doubt recalled that it could contribute some extra pyrazenes and grassiness to sauvignon blanc, qualities rather more admired then than now. Nouvelle has that character in a big way. I doubt if it ever appears in anything other than a blend.

The local crossing that comes next in terms of plantings is roobernet, from cabernet sauvignon and alicante bouschet (the latter itself a French cross), again by Orffer. A fascinating and instructive story about this was recently told on Wine Goggle by Emile Joubert, who discusses the significance of its being the same crossing as the earlier Odesa Black, bred in the Ukraine. It’s a good story (though perhaps Emile and I are both unusually eccentric in finding these minor bits of local wine history fascinating); but I think he’s wrong in concluding that these two are “the same cultivar” and that ruby cab is “not a Stellenbosch invention”. All these crosses involve sexual, not vegetative, reproduction, and crossing the same parents will result in offspring at least as different as human siblings are from one another, and just as worthy of different names. Ruby cab deserves its place on the list – while it’s there, as it is a fading presence, albeit still robust. And it undoubtedly should have been included in the great Jancis Robinson et al book on Wine Grapes, which it is not.

The also-rans of the breeding programme

As to the few other local crossings which linger on but are essentially moribund, there’s nothing much to say, except (seeing as I’m here) to mention them dutifully. Chenel (chenin and ugni blanc, the last bit of its name recalling Elsenburg) was once widely planted but there’s little of it left. Grachen (more pyrozenes, reportedy; I notice the name is more or less an anagram of grenache, but I have no idea if that’s relevant) seems to have been one of the later Orffer offerings, but I’d never even heard of it till perusing these lists. Weldra (Welgevallen + dra (carry/bear)) is another chenin-ugni blanc cross, bred to provide high yields for the brandy industry but clearly in even more dire straits than brandy. Neither of these two made it to Robinson’s Wine Grapes, which seems wrong but not worth making a fuss about as they’re almost dead – though, strangely, at least weldra did appear in Jancis’s much earlier Guide to Wine Grapes.

Good luck to Badenhorst-revived colomino, though my hopes are of the faintest. I do still want to hear more about mysterious brakboseiland, and hope that what appears to be its passing (without ever having been properly noticed!) might not be the case.

  • Tim James is one of South Africa’s leading wine commentators, contributing to various local and international wine publications. His book Wines of the New South Africa – Tradition and Revolution appeared in 2013.

title: Recipe: Goulash soup with spinach and peas
summary:
Hungry? Hungary has the answer. Serves 4 Ingredients: 2 tbsp (30ml) olive oil 2 onions, finely chopped 2 carrots, peeled and roughly chopped 2 celery sticks, finely sliced 2 cloves of garlic, crushed 1 tbsp (15ml) paprika 600g beef goulash, cubed salt and freshly ground pepper pinch of dried chilli flakes (optional) 1 tbsp (15ml) […]

The post Recipe: Goulash soup with spinach and peas appeared first on winemag.
content:
Serve with Lanzerac Pionier Pinotage 2014.

Hungry? Hungary has the answer.

Serves 4

Ingredients:
2 tbsp (30ml) olive oil
2 onions, finely chopped
2 carrots, peeled and roughly chopped
2 celery sticks, finely sliced
2 cloves of garlic, crushed
1 tbsp (15ml) paprika
600g beef goulash, cubed
salt and freshly ground pepper
pinch of dried chilli flakes (optional)
1 tbsp (15ml) tomato paste
1 tin chopped tomatoes
1l beef stock
2 potatoes, peeled and cubed
½ cup (125ml) frozen peas
150g baby spinach
crusty bread to serve

Method:
Heat olive oil in a heavy based pot and sauté onions, carrots, celery and garlic for a few minutes until lightly golden brown.

Add paprika and goulash and brown well.

Season with salt and freshly ground pepper, add chilli and stir in the tomato paste.

Add chopped tomatoes and beef stock and cook over a low heat for 1½ – 2 hours or until the meat is tender.

Add potatoes and cook for a further 15-20 minutes or until almost cooked through.

Add peas and spinach and cook for a couple more minutes or until peas have softened and spinach has wilted.

Check seasoning and serve immediately with crusty bread.

Wine pairing:
A robust, earthy wine is required to stand up to the strong flavours of the dish – try a Pinotage or full-bodied Shiraz.

  • Recipe supplied by Source Food – a Cape Town-based food agency that specializes in experiential marketing. They will create a recipe or meal to communicate your brand’s message.

title: Malu Lambert: South Africa’s growers need a new deal
summary:
South Africa’s wine industry has been built on what critic and commentator Michael Fridjhon describes as “a history of production-driven enterprises”. Speaking at the University of Cape Town’s Business of Wine graduation, he touched on how the industry has evolved from one dominated by growers supplying cooperatives to being increasingly defined by the estate model. The post Malu Lambert: South Africa’s growers need a new deal appeared first on winemag.
content:
South Africa’s wine industry has been built on what critic and commentator Michael Fridjhon describes as “a history of production-driven enterprises”. Speaking at the University of Cape Town’s Business of Wine graduation, he touched on how the industry has evolved from one dominated by growers supplying cooperatives to being increasingly defined by the estate model.

Official figures tell a story of contraction. According to SAWIS, the number of primary grape producers has fallen from 3,667 in 2009 to 2,176 in 2025; a staggering 41% decline. Stellenbosch, despite its concentration of premium estates, has lost almost a third of its growers.

Private wine cellars have also declined, from 524 to 434 over the same period, suggesting broader consolidation across the industry. 

The distinction between growers is important: traditional suppliers to cooperatives, specialist growers for premium brands as well as for independent winemakers, and wine estates growing fruit for their own labels, either on-site or on satellite properties, such as Bosman Family Vineyards’s Hemel-en-Aarde holding.

Sitting beside me at the graduation is Raphaela van Embden, a 2018 graduate of the programme who has since become a co-convener, alongside her work as a content producer. Having graduated the previous year, I myself am back to hand over the class medal.

Michael’s speech gets us talking. Raphaela has recently completed a dissertation, Price Variation of South African Old Vine Grapes According to Social Ties, examining the economics of grape growing, specifically how power and trust influence the prices.

“You can’t bank sentiment”

Drawing on 387 old-vine grape transactions between 2019 and 2024 and interviews with 25 industry participants, Raphaela’s research reveals a disconnect between the perceived value of old vines and the prices the growers receive.

While wines made from old vines command a retail premium of R2.96 for every additional year of vine age, Raphaela found that this has no measurable effect on the price for the grapes themselves.

South Africa’s grape-pricing model is structured around volume rather than quality. Old vines, however, typically produce around 4 tonnes per hectare, compared with an industry average of 18 tonnes for younger vines.

“What struck me was how you can divide grape growers into those who have been able to leverage the reputation of their old-vine grapes, as well as their connection to reputable winemakers; and those who haven’t.”

Her research found that some have moved away from traditional per-tonne pricing altogether, negotiating fixed payments per hectare, with winemakers sharing farming costs.

Instead of carrying the financial risk of lower yields, growers receive an agreed return for maintaining the vineyard to a particular standard. And, winemakers gain secure access to fruit.

“There’s almost this courtship that producers have to undergo,” Raphaela laughs. “Knowing the family, the children and even the dog’s name is important. Trust doesn’t necessarily mean a higher price, but it does open doors.”

And while sentiment keeps many of these vineyards alive… as one grower said to Raphaela: “You can’t bank sentiment.”

Regions are under significant pressure. The Northern Cape for example has lost 71 per cent of its growers between 2009 and 2025.

The cooperatives are also consolidating. Producer cellars and crush facilities, too, continue to drop off the spreadsheet – Stellenbosch and Paarl have seen particularly pronounced declines in private cellars.

The potential it seems is in the newer territories. On the Cape South Coast, private cellars have increased from 47 in 2016 to 59 in 2025, alongside a growing number of (uncalculated) independent brands.

The modern South African wine revolution, it can be argued, was built in part by these kinds of producers: ambitious young winemakers who source fruit without having to own land. But clearly, that model is coming under pressure. So what does the future of grape growing look like?

The future of grape growing

There’s no one better to talk to about this than Danie Carinus, sixth generation grower and co-founder of Carinus Family Vineyards in Stellenbosch’s Polkadraai Hills.

“I doubt whether there are new Basie van Lills coming through,” he says, referring to the legendary Skurfberg grower whose vineyards sprung some of the country’s most celebrated wines. “The only way I now plant vineyards is on an offtake agreement; where I know there’s going to be a home for that fruit”.

After completing a vintage in California in 2006, Danie returned home with the idea that South African growers needed to take greater control of their destinies. At the time, the family supplied virtually all its fruit to Stellenbosch Vineyards. Rather than continuing to depend on a single buyer, he picked up a copy of Platter’s and started calling producers. One of the first to respond was Bruwer Raats. In 2008, Danie planted cabernet franc and malbec for him, fruit that would eventually find its way into MR de Compostella.

The family’s Polkadraai property is approximately 180 hectares, of which around 40 is currently under vine. Danie envisages a smaller, more focused vineyard area and as part of this restructuring, he is planning to establish approximately 30 hectares of new vineyards over the next three years, replacing marginal blocks with sites designed from the outset to produce premium fruit. The programme is being developed in partnership with producers he has long-standing relationships with.

“If we design vineyards from the soil up, the potential for quality is considerably greater.”

Much like the arrangements Raphaela identified in her old-vine research, Danie is exploring agreements in which winemakers contribute towards planting costs, then pay a fixed price per hectare rather than per tonne.

“We already have deals like that in place,” says Danie. “So if we need to drop fruit for quality considerations, we can because we know what we’re getting paid.”

“It’s not a new model. It works in Europe.”

Danie believes such partnerships will become increasingly important as the economics of grape growing continue to deteriorate. “Vines are making way for strawberry tunnels.”

Then there’s own-label producers, whose ability to quickly establish brands has been made possible by under-valued grapes. Danie compares it to a winemaker approaching Domaine de la Romanée-Conti and asking to buy a few rows. “They would laugh at you”.

He questions whether enough of those businesses have subsequently reinvested in the vineyards on which their success depends.

Established producers he says are also a part of the problem having become accustomed to buying premium fruit at prices that don’t adequately reward growers.

“We need to start promoting the wards, the places and the slopes more than we do the growers or the winemakers,” he argues. “In Europe, the vineyards are the heroes. If you make the vineyard the hero, then suddenly grape growing becomes more attractive”.

Things need to change.“Otherwise, there aren’t going to be vineyards left,” he says.

The next generation of vineyards is a question that interests James Downes of Shannon Vineyards in Elgin. He distinguishes between replanting ageing blocks, which simply maintain the existing footprint against the establishment of new vineyards on previously unplanted slopes.

These new sites, he believes, could yield South Africa’s next great discoveries. And where to plant must increasingly take into account water availability, rising temperatures and the potential of cooler, higher-altitude regions.

“Being in the Cape South Coast, I’m biased towards the region’s resilience to global warming as well as the urban sprawl threatening traditional areas.”

During a harvest in Chile he says he was struck by how many wineries sourced grapes beyond their immediate surroundings. He sees a similar trend emerging, citing Elgin wines from Thelema, Tokara, Vrede en Lust and Boschendal as well as Boekenhoutskloof’s Cap Maritime wines in the Hemel-en-Aarde.

“It is very difficult to change the address of a cellar,” he rightly says, “and much easier to plant vineyards or source grapes.”

Prospecting new territories, pricing per hectare rather than per tonne, and valuing vineyards over brands. The recipe seems simple enough, but are these growing pains too much for an industry so comfortable with the status quo?

The proverbial frog in slowly boiling water comes to mind.

  • Malu Lambert is a freelance wine journalist and wine judge who has written for numerous local and international titles. She is a WSET Diploma alum and won the title of Louis Roederer Emerging Wine Writer of the Year 2019, among many other accolades. She sits on various tasting panels and has judged in competitions abroad. Follow her on X: @MaluLambert
